blocks.text: In our view the Hebrew האיה haaja is the same bird as the Arabic اليويو [al-yūyū] aljuju. The bird is so called from its cry. For just as eagles are said to clangere, kites jugere or lipire, hawks pipare, and ravens crocitare, so the proper sound of this bird, according to the Arabs, is يايا [yāyā] jaja, and the cry itself is called اليايا [al-yāyā] aljajao. From this, then, the bird itself seems to have been called in Hebrew איה aja, as in Arabic يويو [yūyū] juju, and in the plural يايي [yāyī] jaji. Nor should it seem strange that a bird's name is taken from its voice, if Varro is right in book 4 of On the Latin Language: Most (birds) are named from their own calls, such as these: upupa, cuculus, corvus, hirundo, ulula, bubo; likewise these: pavo, anser, gallina, columba. Further, اليويو [al-yūyū] aljuju is among the species of hawks; and as Aristotle reckons ten kinds of them and Pliny sixteen, so the Arabs too count many. Among these is the صقر [ṣaqr] sacer, in the vernacular sacre, which is again subdivided into three species, namely the saker properly so called [II, 780] ^{(1)}, the كونج [kawnaj] chauneg, and the يويو [yūyū] juju, of which Damir says: الصنف الثالث من الصغور اليويو وتسميه اهل مصر والشام الجلم لخغة جناحه وسرعته ولان الجلم هو الذي منجز به وهو المقص وهو طاير صغير قصير الذنب ومزاجه بالنسبة الي الباشق بارد رطب لانه اصبر منه نغسا واثغل حركة ويشرب الما شربا ضروريا كما يشربه الباسق الا انه ابخر ومزاجه بالنسبة الي الصغر حار يابس واذلك هو اشجع منه ويغال ان اول من ضراه واصطاد به بهرام جور وذلك انه شاهد يويو يطارد قبرة ويراوغها ويترفع وينخغض معها وما تركها الي ان صادها فاعجبه ذلك وامر به فادب وصاد به [al-ṣinf al-thālith min al-ṣughūr al-yūyū wa-tusammīhi ahl Miṣr wa-l-Shām al-jalam li-khiffat janāḥihi wa-surʿatihi wa-li-anna al-jalam huwa alladhī munjaz bihi wa-huwa al-miqaṣṣ wa-huwa ṭāyir ṣaghīr qaṣīr al-dhanab wa-mizājuhu bi-l-nisba ilā al-bāshiq bārid raṭb li-annahu aṣbar minhu nafasan wa-athqal ḥarakatan wa-yashrab al-mā shurban ḍarūriyyan kamā yashrabuhu al-bāsiq illā annahu abkhar wa-mizājuhu bi-l-nisba ilā al-ṣaqr ḥārr yābis wa-li-dhālika huwa ashjaʿ minhu wa-yuqāl anna awwal man ḍarrāhu wa-iṣṭāda bihi Bahrām Jūr wa-dhālika annahu shāhada yūyū yuṭārid qubbara wa-yurāwighuhā wa-yatarafaʿ wa-yankhafiḍ maʿahā wa-mā tarakahā ilā an ṣādahā fa-aʿjabahu dhālika wa-amara bihi fa-uddiba wa-ṣāda bihi] [col. 194] The third species of SAKERS is aljuju, which the Egyptians and Syrians call algelem, because of the lightness and swiftness of its wings. For algelem means a sickle, or one furnished with a sickle (as though it cut the air with its wings as with a sickle). It is a small bird with a short tail. If you compare its temperament with that of albasik (another kind of hawk), it is cold and moist, because it holds its breath longer and is heavier in movement, and it drinks water when it must, as albasik drinks; yet it is more foul-smelling than it. But if you compare it with the saker (properly so called), it will appear to be of a hot and dry temperament, and is accordingly bolder than it. Moreover, a certain man named Behram Giur is said to have been the first to use it for hunting. For when, in his presence, a juju bird had pursued a lark and grappled with it, rising and descending with it, and not leaving it until it had caught it, he marvelled at this, ordered the bird to be trained, and afterwards used it for hunting. So far Damir. From this it is clear that the bird described is the one called in German Smirle, in Italian smerlo and smeriglio, in French esmerillon [merlin]. For it too is reckoned among the species of hawks and falcons. But in size it is the smallest (says Albertus, book 23, chapter 14), yet it yields to none in spirit and daring, in proportion to its body and strength, etc. Thus William the Falconer reports that he once caught a crane by means of these birds. Otherwise it can overcome only larks and similar birds [II, 781] etc. Its wings are very long in relation to its body, its tail moderate (that is, of middling size), its legs and feet flat, etc. They are very swift and crafty, and in taking their prey they ascend, and descend as they strike, etc. And Crescentiensis: The Ismerli are like falconelli, that is, little falcons, which they resemble both in shape of body and in colour of plumage, etc. They take chiefly larks, which they pursue with such eagerness and impetus that they sometimes dash even against a burning oven, or into a well, or against men's clothing. Another writer in Gesner: The Smerillo has the form of a falcon, is smaller than the sparrowhawk, and flies faster than any other bird. It takes the same birds as the sparrowhawk, but especially small ones, such as the sparrow, the lark and the like ^{(2)}. You see, reader, that like the Arabs' aljuju, our smirlus or smerillon belongs to the hawk species, is small in stature, short-tailed, swift in flight, remarkable for daring, and especially given to hunting larks; so that there can be no doubt at all that the same bird is designated by different names. But another point must above all be noted, because it bears most on our subject. If someone has lively and very keen eyes, the French say by a common proverb that he has the eyes of a smerillon, because this bird has such eyes. And the Arab poets too greatly praise the eyes of their juju. Among them an anonymous poet in Damir:
يويو مهذب رشيق ۞ كان عينيه لذي التحقيق ۞ فصان مخروطان من عقيق ۞ [yūyū muhadhdhab rashīq ۞ ka-anna ʿaynayhi li-dhī al-taḥqīq ۞ faṣṣān makhrūṭān min ʿaqīq ۞]

The Iuju is swift and nimble (in flight), whose eyes are truly lovely, and its pupils, as if polished on the lathe, more than sapphire. And Abu Nuwas, in his work On Fowling, entitled طريدة [Ṭarīda] Tarida, says of the same bird, among other things:
ازرق لا تكذب عيناه ۞ فلا يري القانص ما يراه ۞ [azraq lā takdhib ʿaynāhu ۞ fa-lā yarā al-qāniṣ mā yarāhu ۞]
